title: The Lydian Mode, an Explainer
content_blocks: The Lydian mode is nearly identical to the major mode, except that the fourth scale degree is raised. Raising scale degree four pulls the notes in the mode toward scale degree five—whereas in the major mode the pull is inevitably and inexorably to scale degree one (the tonic), that pull toward five reduces the strength of, and sense of finality ordinarily associated with, the tonic.

It also changes the nature of the harmonies available.  In the major mode, the chord built on scale degree five is a “dominant seventh,” which has a very strong drive to resolve to the major chord built on scale degree one.  But raising scale degree four in the Lydian mode changes that dominant seventh to a major seventh chord, identical in quality to what can be built on the tonic scale degree.  This relationship can give the music a sort of frozen, or non-directional quality.

At the same time, unlike any of the other newly-created modes, all of the scale degrees are only a step apart—there are no leaps built in to the mode. This means that when the fugue melodies are transposed to other scale degrees or higher or lower registers, the melodies remain largely intact and stable. For Prelude-and-Fugue No.13, although the C tonality is undermined by raised scale-degree four, the stability of the entire piece and the repetitions of the chords in the prelude and postlude sections answer the tonal instability of the previous prelude and fugue, and round off the entire set.
The Lydian mode…gives the music a sort of frozen, non-directional quality.
